questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: One secret used in both directions
questions.learningObjective: Identify the property that makes one shared key safe for two-way traffic
questions.stem: A design brief describes two regional offices that must share one key so each can read what the other sends. Which statement best describes this arrangement?

options.text: Both offices hold one key and use it for encryption and for decryption
Each office holds a private key and sends only the public half over the wire
options.misconception: mistakes a shared secret for a public-key scheme

options.text: The key is rebuilt from a passphrase each time a session starts
options.misconception: believes a passphrase removes the need to protect the key

options.text: The key is hidden inside the client program, so nobody can read it
options.misconception: believes hiding a key in code is enough to protect it

questions.explanation: One key is used in both directions, so both endpoints hold the same secret and protect it equally. The tempting public-key option invents a second key, and hiding a key in client code only relocates the risk.
questions.hint: Ask which direction the single key travels in.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Changing a shared value without losing the link
questions.learningObjective: Select the key handling that keeps a rotated secret compatible with older clients
questions.stem: A partner integration brief describes rotating the shared signing secret. Traffic signed with the retired key still arrives during a grace window. What must the receiver do?

options.text: Try the incoming tag against the retired key only, since only retired keys still arrive
options.misconception: checks a single old key and still fails new traffic

options.text: Try the incoming tag against every key it still keeps, so older traffic still verifies
Accept any tag that matches the newest key and skip checks when the key id is unknown
options.misconception: skips verification when the key identifier is unfamiliar

options.text: Reject every message whose key id is not the newest, since older tags cannot be trusted
options.misconception: assumes any key other than the newest is compromised

questions.explanation: During a grace window the receiver keeps both the retiring and the new secret, so each incoming tag can be tried against every key it still holds. The tempting strict option rejects legitimate older clients and the lenient option drops verification entirely.
questions.hint: Keep the old key alive for the whole grace window.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Publishing one half in the open
questions.learningObjective: Explain the capabilities that a published key half grants and withholds
questions.stem: A notice board service publishes one half of a key pair openly while the other half stays on its server. Explain what a reader can do with the published half and what cannot be done.

answer.exemplar: The published half is the public key: anyone can encrypt a message that only the holder of the private half can open, and anyone can check a signature made with the private half. It cannot be used to decrypt traffic that was encrypted for the owner, and it reveals nothing about the private half.

questions.explanation: Publishing the public half lets anyone verify signatures and seal messages for the owner without giving away the private half. The tempting wrong idea treats the public half as if it could decrypt or as if it could sign.
questions.hint: Think about which half performs each operation.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What must be true for a signature to mean anything
questions.learningObjective: Compute the length of a signature produced by a given key size
questions.stem: A firmware brief specifies a 2048-bit signing key and states that each release carries the raw signature value. How many bytes does that signature occupy?
questions.explanation: A raw signature is as long as the modulus, so 2048 bits equal 256 bytes. The tempting answer sizes it by the digest, which would be 64 bytes for a 512-bit hash.
questions.hint: Convert the key size from bits to bytes.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What a signature leaves unestablished
questions.learningObjective: Identify what a valid signature does not prove

stimulus.body: A deployment brief states that a signed build proves the update came from the release key and has not changed since signing. It says nothing about defects in the code or about who else may hold a copy of the signing key.

questions.stem: On the basis of the brief, which claim is not established by a valid signature on the build?

options.text: That the update bytes are the same bytes that were signed, since any change alters the digest
options.misconception: believes the signature also certifies the content is harmless

options.text: That the signer held the private key, since producing the signature requires it
options.misconception: believes the signer identity alone proves the code is sound

options.text: That the build is free of defects and safe to deploy, since signing says nothing about quality
That the update came from an authorised party, since only the key holder can sign
options.misconception: believes a valid signature guarantees the payload is defect-free

questions.explanation: A signature binds bytes to a key holder and detects later edits; it says nothing about whether the code is correct or safe. The tempting options all describe real properties of signing and therefore read as if they were the missing one.
questions.hint: Signing authenticates bytes, it does not judge them.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Producing a signature and checking it
questions.learningObjective: State the correct signing and verification steps in order
questions.stem: A brief asks for a two-step procedure. The sender signs a document, then a checker recovers a value and compares it with the digest of the document. Which option states both steps correctly?

options.text: Compute the document digest with the private key, then check that digest against the file
options.misconception: treats a plain digest as if it required the private key

options.text: Encrypt the document with the public key, then decrypt it with the private key to recover it
options.misconception: describes encryption with the public key instead of signing

options.text: Hash the document with the private key, then hash the recovered value with the public key
options.misconception: believes the private key performs the hashing step

options.text: Compute the digest and sign it with the private key, then recover and compare it with the public key

questions.explanation: Signing hashes the message and encrypts that hash with the private key; verification uses the public key to recover the hash and compares it. The tempting options mix hashing with key operations or reverse the key roles.
questions.hint: Ask which key does the signing and which does the checking.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: A digest anyone can compute
questions.learningObjective: Describe what a plain digest reveals and what it fails to prove
questions.stem: An indexing brief says the service stores only a hash of each uploaded document and keeps no secret. Which statement about that stored hash is correct?

options.text: Anyone with the document can compute the same hash, so it detects edits but not origin
Only a holder of a secret key can reproduce the stored hash, so it also proves origin
options.misconception: confuses a plain digest with a keyed tag

options.text: The hash cannot be recomputed from the document, so a reader cannot check it
options.misconception: believes a digest hides the input it came from

options.text: The hash is as long as the document, so it stores the same space as the file
options.misconception: assumes the digest length grows with the input

questions.explanation: A plain digest is computable by anyone from the same input, so it detects changes without proving who produced the data. The tempting keyed option adds a secret the brief explicitly says is not kept.
questions.hint: Nothing secret is involved in a plain hash.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: A tag that needs a key
questions.learningObjective: Identify which recorded result proves a keyed tag was produced
questions.stem: A pipeline brief records integrity results for three shipped artefacts, two with a keyed tag and one with a plain digest. Which recorded result shows the keyed tag doing its job?

options.text: The digest of the third artefact, because it was computed with no key material
options.misconception: treats a plain digest as evidence that the key was used

options.text: The tag of the second artefact, because recomputing it with the key reproduces it
The length of the first tag, because a correct tag always has one fixed size
options.misconception: believes tag length proves the key was applied

options.text: The order the tags were created, because only the sender knows the right sequence
options.misconception: assumes creation order carries proof of key use

questions.explanation: A keyed tag can only be reproduced by someone who holds the key, so recomputing it and getting the same value is the evidence that matters. A plain digest, a length and an ordering are all reproducible or unchanged without the key.
questions.hint: Only the key holder can reproduce the tag.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: One secret used in both directions
questions.learningObjective: Explain the mutual protection and mutual risk of a shared key
questions.stem: A support line brief says the technician and the customer agent share one secret used in both directions. Explain what the arrangement gives each party and what it costs each party.

answer.exemplar: Each party can protect what it sends and check what it receives using a single secret rather than a pair of keys. The cost is symmetric responsibility: whoever leaks the secret can read and forge the other side's traffic, and neither party can show a third party which of them produced a given message.

questions.explanation: A single shared secret gives both sides confidentiality and tamper detection on the same footing. The tempting wrong idea treats the shared secret as if it gave one side more protection or better proof of origin than the other.
questions.hint: Both sides hold identical material, so both sides carry identical risk.

questions.topic: Changing a shared value without losing the link
questions.learningObjective: Count the key versions that remain usable after a rotation
questions.stem: A brief assigns sequential key identifiers from 1 to 7 to a shared secret. Identifier 1 is retired and identifier 7 becomes active today. How many identifiers are in current use?
questions.explanation: Identifiers 2 through 6 remain in current use, which is five of them. The tempting count of seven treats the retired identifier 1 or the not yet active identifier 7 as still in service.
questions.hint: Exclude the retired identifier and the one not yet active.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Publishing one half in the open
questions.learningObjective: Judge whether a published key half can serve a verification-only fleet

stimulus.body: A device fleet brief requires every unit to check update signatures without holding any secret, while only the build server can produce them. The brief permits the public half to be shipped inside the firmware image.

questions.stem: Given the brief, what property must the shipped public half have for the fleet check to mean anything?

options.text: It must equal the private half, so that any unit can also produce signatures
options.misconception: believes the two halves must share one value

options.text: It must be secret from the devices, so an attacker cannot check whether it works
options.misconception: confuses a public key with a secret key

options.text: It must pair with a private half held only by the signer, so only the signer can sign
It must be hashed, so its value can be recovered from a signature alone
options.misconception: believes the public half must be pre-hashed

questions.explanation: The fleet can only trust a check if the public half it holds genuinely belongs to the signer, which means the matching private half stays with the signer. The tempting options treat the halves as identical, secret or pre-hashed, none of which is true.
questions.hint: Ask who can create a signature that verifies against it.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What must be true for a signature to mean anything
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a signature must cover the exact bytes being installed
questions.stem: A brief requires a signed release to pass two conditions before installation: the signature must verify, and it must cover the exact image bytes. What does the second condition achieve?

options.text: It confirms the image was downloaded over a secure channel at install time
options.misconception: confuses signing with transport security

options.text: It proves the image contains no defects, which a signature can never check
options.misconception: believes signing certifies software quality

options.text: It shows the image was built on the release server rather than a developer laptop
options.misconception: believes a signature proves where code was built

options.text: It binds the signature to those bytes, so substituting other bytes breaks the check

questions.explanation: The signature covers the digest of the image, so the check binds the approval to those exact bytes and any substitution changes the digest. The tempting options describe things a signature cannot establish at all, such as quality, channel or build location.
questions.hint: Substituting bytes must break the verification.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What a signature leaves unestablished
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish what signing adds on a channel that carries plaintext
questions.stem: A notice brief says announcements travel in the clear but are digitally signed so readers can identify the issuer. Which statement describes what signing adds on that channel?

options.text: Signing links the announcement to the issuer while leaving the words readable by anyone
Signing encrypts the announcement so that only intended readers can recover it
options.misconception: treats a signature as if it provided confidentiality

options.text: Signing confirms that the announcement was delivered to every subscriber in the fleet
options.misconception: believes signing tracks delivery to subscribers

options.text: Signing prevents a captured announcement from being stored and replayed later
options.misconception: believes a signature blocks replay attacks by itself

questions.explanation: On a clear channel the signature contributes provenance and tamper detection only; the payload stays readable by anyone who intercepts it. The tempting options add confidentiality, delivery confirmation or replay protection, none of which a signature provides.
questions.hint: Signing answers who sent it, not who can read it.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Producing a signature and checking it
questions.learningObjective: Read verification logs and identify a genuine pass
questions.stem: A brief records four verification attempts against firmware updates. Which recorded outcome shows the checking step working as the brief specifies?

options.text: The first update passed because its file name matched the expected release suffix
options.misconception: confuses a file name check with signature verification

options.text: The third update passed because the recovered value matched the digest of its bytes
The second update passed because it carried a longer signature than the other updates
options.misconception: believes signature length indicates validity

options.text: The fourth update passed because it was fetched from a mirror the team trusts
options.misconception: treats a trusted mirror as proof of authenticity

questions.explanation: Verification passes only when the value recovered with the public key equals the digest recomputed from the bytes received. A file name, a signature length and a trusted download host are all weak proxies that an attacker can satisfy.
questions.hint: The recovered value must equal the recomputed digest.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: A digest anyone can compute
questions.learningObjective: Explain why recomputable digests need a trusted place to be stored
questions.stem: An audit brief archives records together with their digests so later readers can tell whether the records were altered. Explain why an attacker who can write to the archive could change a record without being caught.

answer.exemplar: The digest is computed from the record alone, so anyone able to rewrite the record can also recompute and store the digest that matches it. Detection only works when the stored digest sits somewhere the attacker cannot rewrite, such as an append-only log or a separately published list.

questions.explanation: Because the digest is recomputable by anyone, integrity checking only works when the reference value is stored somewhere the attacker cannot alter. The tempting wrong idea is that hashing alone makes tampering impossible, which it does not.
questions.hint: Ask where the old digest is kept.

questions.learningObjective: Compute the overhead added by a tag, a nonce and a length field
questions.stem: A brief states that every message carries a 12-byte authentication tag, a 9-byte nonce and a 4-byte length field outside the message body. How many bytes of overhead do those fields add?
questions.explanation: The three fields add 12 plus 9 plus 4 bytes, which is 25 bytes of overhead. The tempting answer counts only the tag and forgets the nonce and the length field the brief lists.
questions.hint: Add the three field sizes together.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: One secret used in both directions
questions.learningObjective: Identify the extra protection a counter adds to a shared key link

stimulus.body: A sensor link brief says each link uses one pre-shared key and that every frame carries a counter so the receiver can notice a frame it has already handled. The same key is used to protect both directions of the link.

questions.stem: Given the brief, what does the counter defend against that the shared key alone does not?

options.text: It reveals the plaintext of a frame that an outsider captured earlier on the link
options.misconception: believes a counter decrypts captured traffic

options.text: It makes it impossible for an outsider to copy the key out of the device hardware
options.misconception: confuses replay protection with key protection

options.text: It lets the receiver reject a frame that it has already processed once before
It proves to the receiver that the sending device is the one the brief names
options.misconception: assumes a counter authenticates the sender

questions.explanation: The key proves a frame was produced by someone holding the secret, while the counter lets the receiver notice a frame being presented twice. The tempting options confuse a replay guard with decryption, key extraction or sender identity.
questions.hint: The key stops forgery; the counter stops repeats.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Changing a shared value without losing the link
questions.learningObjective: Explain the purpose of a key version identifier during rotation
questions.stem: A brief describes two stages of a key rotation. Both ends first agree which key version is in force, then each frame names the version it was protected under. Why is the second stage needed?

options.text: It encrypts the version identifier so that outsiders cannot see which key is in force
options.misconception: believes the key identifier must be confidential

options.text: It proves to the receiver that the sender holds the secret for the named version
options.misconception: confuses a version tag with proof of possession

options.text: It lets the receiver mint a fresh key for the next session by itself
options.misconception: assumes the receiver can derive new keys alone

options.text: It lets the receiver choose the right key for a frame built under an earlier version

questions.explanation: During a changeover the receiver may hold several secrets, so the version label tells it which one to test and lets both old and new frames succeed. The tempting options add confidentiality, possession proof or key generation, none of which a label provides.
questions.hint: The label selects the key, it does not prove anything.

questions.topic: Publishing one half in the open
questions.learningObjective: Describe the rights that separate key halves give each party
questions.stem: A ticket brief says the verification key sits inside the reader application while the signing key stays on a server in a locked room. What does that separation allow?

options.text: Only the server can create valid tickets while any reader can check them
Both the server and anyone with the reader application can create valid tickets
options.misconception: thinks embedding a key shares the signing ability

options.text: Any person can create valid tickets because the verification key is published
options.misconception: assumes a public key grants signing rights

options.text: Nobody can create valid tickets because the verification key is buried in the code
options.misconception: believes embedding a key makes it secret

questions.explanation: The half that verifies can be handed out freely because it cannot sign, while the half that signs must stay on the server. The tempting options mistake publication for signing rights or assume that hiding a key in code protects it.
questions.hint: Ask which half can create the artefact.

questions.topic: What must be true for a signature to mean anything
questions.learningObjective: Select the artefact state that a correct verifier would accept
questions.stem: A brief lists the state of four signed artefacts. Which state would a verifier working to that brief accept?

options.text: The signature verifies under the release key but was computed over the source archive
options.misconception: misses that the digest must cover the installed bytes

options.text: The signature verifies under the release key and covers the bytes that will be installed
The signature does not verify but the file name matches an approved release pattern
options.misconception: treats a name pattern as an authenticity check

options.text: The signature verifies only after the build server's retired key is added to the trust list
options.misconception: believes any key added to a list can validate

questions.explanation: Acceptance needs a signature that verifies under the trusted release key and covers the exact bytes to be installed. The tempting options each miss the binding to the installed bytes or the verification step itself.
questions.hint: Both the key and the bytes must line up.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What a signature leaves unestablished
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a signature alone does not fix the identity of the signer
questions.stem: A contract workflow brief claims a signature proves the signer's identity and that the document is unchanged. Explain why the signature alone does not establish who the signer was.

answer.exemplar: A signature shows that whoever produced it held the private key, but the public key in the brief is not yet tied to a real person. Until the key is bound to an identity through a trusted record, an outsider cannot separate the legitimate signer from anyone holding a copy of the same key, so attribution rests entirely on that binding.

questions.explanation: A signature binds a message to a key, and only a trusted binding from that key to a person can support a claim about identity. The tempting wrong idea treats the possession of the key as if it were proof of the person.
questions.hint: The key must be tied to a person by some trusted record.

questions.stem: Under the brief, what does publishing only the name of the digest algorithm allow a reader of the archive to do?

options.text: Recover the original contents of any file in the archive from the stored digest
options.misconception: believes a digest can be reversed into the original file

options.text: Edit a file in the archive and recompute a matching digest so the change goes unseen
options.misconception: overstates what an attacker can do without rewriting the chain

options.text: Recompute the digest of any file they can obtain and compare it with the stored value
Use the stored digest as a key that decrypts the rest of the archive
options.misconception: confuses a digest with encryption key material

questions.explanation: Publishing the algorithm lets anyone recompute a digest from a file they already hold and check it against the stored value. The tempting options claim reversal, invisible editing or decryption, which the digest does not allow.

questions.stem: A brief says the receiver must re-derive the authentication tag over the received message and compare it with the tag that arrived. Which failure is this step able to catch?

options.text: That the message was compressed on disk by the sender before transmission
options.misconception: confuses a transport artefact with a forgery

options.text: That the sender used an older version of the message format
options.misconception: believes tags depend on format versions

options.text: That the network delivered the message more slowly than the target allows
options.misconception: thinks a timing difference indicates tampering

options.text: That the body was altered in transit or that the tag was produced without the key

The shared secret is stronger because both firms then hold identical copies of it
options.misconception: believes holding identical copies increases strength

options.text: The two-secret design is stronger because a shared secret is published in the open
options.misconception: claims a shared secret is published openly

options.text: Both designs are equivalent because only the length of a secret decides its strength
options.misconception: reduces secret strength to length alone

questions.topic: Publishing one half in the open
questions.learningObjective: Explain why replacing a published half need not change a signing key
questions.stem: A public directory brief rotates the container that carries the published half every year while the signing key itself stays untouched. Explain why replacing the published half does not require changing the signing key.

answer.exemplar: The published half and the signing key are separate pieces of material, so a new container can carry the same published half without touching the key that does the signing. The danger runs the other way: if the signing key changed, every verifier still holding the old published half would reject valid signatures.

questions.explanation: Republishing a public half is a distribution change, whereas changing the signing key changes what valid signatures look like. The tempting wrong idea treats the two halves as inseparable parts of one rotating pair.
questions.hint: One half is distributed, the other does the signing.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What a signature leaves unestablished
questions.learningObjective: Assess what a signature says about the time it was made

stimulus.body: A log archive brief says releases are signed and each signature carries the time it was made. The brief notes that the signing service sets its clock by hand once a year and that the clock is rarely checked afterwards.

questions.stem: Given that the signing clock is rarely checked, what can a verifier conclude about the time recorded inside a signature?

options.text: Nothing dependable, because an unchecked clock may be wrong and the signature cannot fix it
options.misconception: believes an unchecked clock still yields a sound timestamp

options.text: That the release was signed within an hour of that time, because the clock is always right

questions.learningObjective: Explain the benefit and cost of separate keys per direction
questions.stem: A brief weighs giving each direction of a link its own key against using one key for both. Explain what separation buys the design and what it costs.

answer.exemplar: Separating the two directions means a message captured on one side cannot be reflected back as a valid message on the other, which removes a class of attack on protocols that reuse one key. The cost is two keys to distribute and manage instead of one, and both still have to be protected with equal care.

questions.explanation: Separate keys stop a captured message being reflected into the other direction, at the cost of more material to manage. The tempting wrong idea claims separation weakens each direction or removes the need to protect either key.
questions.hint: Think about reflecting one direction into the other.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Changing a shared value without losing the link
questions.learningObjective: Compute the total acceptance period for a rotated shared key
questions.stem: A brief says each shared key is replaced every 90 days and that a replaced key stays accepted for a further 90 days of overlap. For how many days in total can one key be accepted?
questions.explanation: A key is used for its own 90 days and then remains accepted for another 90 days of overlap, giving 180 days. The tempting answer of 90 counts only the overlap window and forgets the period of normal use.
questions.hint: Add the period of use and the overlap window.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Publishing one half in the open
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a published half must never be used to sign

stimulus.body: A settlement brief states that one half of the key pair is published so that card networks can confirm that a settlement file came from the service. The brief forbids the service from ever using that published half to sign anything.

questions.stem: Why does the brief forbid the service from signing with the published half?

options.text: Because a published half would let anyone read the settlement files that the service signs
options.misconception: claims publication exposes the plaintext of signed files

options.text: Because a published half is too slow to sign the settlement files within the required window
options.misconception: blames speed for the prohibition

options.text: Because signing with a published half would let anyone produce signatures that verify against it
Because the card networks only accept signatures of exactly 256 bytes in length
options.misconception: invents a size rule from the networks

questions.explanation: The published half must stay a verification tool only, because anyone holding it could otherwise create signatures that verify against it. The tempting options claim it exposes plaintext, is too slow or faces a size rule, none of which the brief states.
questions.hint: Ask what a stranger holding that half could produce.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What must be true for a signature to mean anything
questions.learningObjective: Identify the failure that only a key approval check can catch
questions.stem: A brief defines acceptance of a signed policy in two stages. Stage one checks the signature against the policy bytes; stage two checks that the signing key appears on the approved list. Which failure can only stage two catch?

options.text: A policy edited after signing, so its digest no longer matches the signature
options.misconception: describes the failure stage one is meant to catch

options.text: A policy stored on a disk that later suffered a hardware fault
options.misconception: invents a storage fault as a verification failure

options.text: A signature computed over a different policy than the one that was delivered
options.misconception: repeats the digest binding failure instead of key approval

options.text: A key that was withdrawn from the approved list, where the signature still verifies under it

questions.explanation: A key can verify perfectly and still be one the organisation has withdrawn, so only the approval list can catch that case. The tempting options restate what stage one or stage two already handles or invent a storage fault.
questions.hint: Signature validity says nothing about whether the key is still approved.
